name: Pompeian Blue
lede: Pompeian blue is an old name for Egyptian blue, the ancient copper-calcium silicate pigment, and was also borrowed for some weak synthetic lakes.

sections.title: A synonym for Egyptian blue
sections.body:
Paterson describes [[egyptian-blue]] as an ancient rich purplish blue or turquoise made by heating copper, lime and quartz, and says it is sometimes called Pompeian blue [1]. It adds that this may have been the first synthetic pigment, a claim it makes with a "perhaps" [1]. Its own entry for Pompeian blue simply sends the reader to Egyptian blue [1].

The Pigment Compendium agrees: it calls Pompeian blue a synonym for the synthetic calcium copper silicate listed by Mayer in 1991 [2]. It also notes that the term was used for certain impermanent synthetic lakes that resemble Egyptian blue in hue [2]. So the name could mean the durable ancient pigment or a fugitive modern imitation.

sections.title: Not to be confused with Pompeian red
sections.body: Paterson also records Pompeian red, a red tied to Pompeii's wall paintings, and sends that entry to [[venetian-red]] [1]. The two names share a place but not a material.

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: The swatch is a grey-blue, not the vivid blue of Egyptian blue, since the library value is a screen approximation [3]. In our archive 374 of 23,781 paintings, about 1.6%, carry a color within a close match of it covering at least 5% of the canvas [4]. Friedrich's *Northern Landscape, Spring* of 1825 is the strongest, at about 61% of the canvas [4].
